newsitem.title: USA: IBM stock soars after surprising earnings report.
newsitem.headline: IBM stock soars after surprising earnings report.

text.p: IBM stock jumped 8 percent in heavy trading Thursday after its first-quarter profits impressed Wall Street, with results pointing to balanced revenues and good cost controls.

The stock of International Business Machines Corp., one of the most widely held by professional money managers and small investors, jumped $11.25 to $153.625 on the New York Stock Exchange. It was the most active issue on the exchange and one of the biggest percentage gainers.

IBM's net income of $1.19 billion, or $2.37 a share, for the quarter beat the consensus First Call analyst forecast of $2.28 a share despite a big decline in its most profitable hardware lines: mainframes and the AS/400 minicomputer family.
IBM benefited from faster growth in other businesses, expense controls and a lower tax rate.
SoundView Financial analyst Gary Helmig said IBM demonstrated "exquisite fiancial management" in the quarter.
"The company's point was that the strength of its portfolio of businesses is showing through," said Steve Milunovich, a Morgan Stanley analyst.

"For example, the company was able to offset paltry mainframe MIPS (a measure of processing power shipped) growth of 6 percent with success in businesses such as hard disks. ... Inconsistencies in individual businesses net out for overall consistency."
He raised his IBM earnings estimates slightly due to the company's lower tax rate.
Helmig said IBM was managing a difficult transition to lower-margin, faster-growing businesses, from slower-growing businesses with higher profit margins.

"They have had a tough transformation going on," Helmig said. "As the higher-margin businesses are languishing, they are switching to lower-margin, higher-growth business, yet they were able to get stockholder earnings growth."
Analysts said IBM's expense controls offset the pressures on its profit margins as its hardware gross profit margins fell to 32.4 percent of revenues vs. 35.1 percent a year ago.

Analysts cautioned, however, that the strong dollar will continue to hurt results for the rest of the year. One analyst, Andrew Neff of Bear Stearns, lowered his earnings estimates, based on the stronger dollar. IBM said its earnings took a 19-cent-a-share hit due to the dollar.
A stronger dollar makes sales in foreign currencies worth less in dollar terms.
"Currency is going to be tougher than expected," said John Jones, a Salomon Brothers analyst.

He added, however, that IBM had had the opportunity to influence analysts to lower estimates for the year, but its chief financial officer, Richard Thoman, said he was comfortable with analysts' current financial models.
